first_impression.reaction: The title is a bit clickbait, 'traditions you did not know' is the sort of thing I scroll past on Pinterest. But the intro wins me back straight away. It admits most lists are recycled and promises sources, and it flags the Standesamt step for Australians, which is the thing I'd actually worry about. James's mum has German family, so I kept going.

journey.quote: What Are the German Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
journey.reaction: A bit listicle. It doesn't sound like the rest of the article, which is much more grown-up than the headline.

journey.quote: Where a story is only "often told", we say so.
journey.reaction: Love this. Honest about what's folklore and what's fact. That's the opposite of the fairytale stuff we usually get.

journey.quote: Plan where the porcelain will be broken and who supplies the brooms, since the clean-up is part of the custom.
journey.reaction: Exactly the kind of practical detail I want. It reads like someone who has actually run one of these.

journey.quote: For a destination wedding in Germany, that makes the Polterabend a natural welcome party for local friends and family.
journey.reaction: Useful idea, but half our guests are flying in from Sydney. How does a welcome party work when they're jet-lagged and staying somewhere different? That's what I'd actually want planned for me.

journey.quote: So plan in that order: secure the Standesamt first, then build the church, garden or castle celebration around it.
journey.reaction: Clear and actionable. This is the line I'd screenshot for James. Confidence on the legal side is one of our big things.

journey.section: What an Australian couple should check
journey.quote: It is applied for only through the Standesamt when you register the marriage, decided by the President of the Higher Regional Court (Oberlandesgericht) for that district, and valid for six months.
journey.reaction: Very thorough, but my eyes are glazing a bit. As a lawyer I appreciate it's precise. As a bride I mostly want to know someone else will handle it.

journey.section: What an Australian couple should check
journey.quote: Notice periods, the full document list, translations and whether the ceremony can be held in English are all set locally, so check with the Standesamt where you plan to marry.
journey.reaction: Honest, but it leaves me with homework. Whether it can be in English is a real question for our grandparents. I'd like at least a sense of how long this takes.

journey.section: Getting married in Germany from Australia
journey.quote: This section is general information, not legal advice. Your Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements with the Standesamt in writing before you book.
journey.reaction: This is the bit that matters. 'In writing before you book' is a real promise, not 'end-to-end' waffle.

journey.section: Getting married in Germany from Australia
journey.quote: One person works in your time zone and plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments with you, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: This answers the 'what does end-to-end actually mean' question better than most planner sites. One accountable person, fee agreed up front. That speaks to both of our fears.

journey.quote: They have to push and pull in rhythm or the saw jams, which is the point: it stands for the co-operation a marriage needs.
journey.reaction: Charming and not cheesy. I could see us doing this without looking try-hard, if it's done well.

journey.quote: At some point after the ceremony, close friends "kidnap" the bride and take her from bar to bar while the groom tries to find them, sometimes leaving him the bill.
journey.reaction: Fun to read, but honestly I'd want someone to tell me which of these come across as dated or awkward with international guests. The article lists them but doesn't really help me choose.

journey.quote: It makes a lovely story for a speech, even if the shoes are paid for by card.
journey.reaction: Cute, but slightly confusing straight after being told German weddings don't really do speeches. Minor.

journey.quote: We found no source we would stand behind on Swiss wedding customs, so for a wedding in Switzerland, ask your venue and your families.
journey.reaction: Weirdly this makes me trust them more. They'd rather say nothing than make it up.

journey.section: Planning a wedding with German roots
journey.quote: Whether you are honouring a German grandmother with a Polterabend in Sydney or marrying at a Standesamt in Bavaria, choose the customs that mean something to your family and leave the rest.
journey.reaction: Nice, personal close. It acknowledges we might not even marry in Germany. Low-pressure ending, which I prefer.

unanswered_questions: Have you actually planned a wedding in Germany? Is there a real wedding with venue and date I can look at?
Roughly how far ahead do we need to start the Standesamt paperwork, so we know if 14 months is comfortable?
Can the Standesamt ceremony be done in English, or do we need an interpreter for our families?
Can the civil and the celebration happen on the same day, and how do you handle that for guests travelling from Australia?
How do you look after older guests flying into Germany, airport to venue?
Which of these customs work well with a mixed international guest list, and which feel dated?
Who is on the ground in Germany on the day if something goes wrong, given the advisor is in our time zone?

turn_offs_found.quote: What Are the German Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
turn_offs_found.why: Clickbait-style headline. Doesn't match the careful, sourced tone of the body and is the sort of thing I'd expect from a content farm.

would_share_with: James's mum (German side of the family)

cta_reaction.quote: If the paperwork is the part keeping you up at night, speak with a Wedded Advisor.
cta_reaction.why: It's soft and well placed right after the legal section, and the 'one person, fee in writing' line is reassuring. But we haven't picked a destination and I'd want to see a real wedding first. I'd bookmark it, read a couple more posts and come back.

top_3_changes: Retitle so it matches the article's grown-up, sourced tone, something plain like a guide to German wedding traditions and what they mean, rather than 'you did not know'.

Add a short note on guest logistics for a destination wedding in Germany (international guests at a Polterabend or welcome party, getting older relatives to the venue), and link to a real wedding with venue and date if one exists.
Give a little help choosing: one or two lines on which customs translate well for an international guest list and which might feel dated, so it reads as a menu with advice rather than a list.
